record_type_quote:
We provide a reappraisal of Tal and Wansink’s study “Blinded with Science”, where seemingly trivial charts were shown
       to increase belief in drug efficacy, presumably because charts are associated with science. Through a series of four replications
       conducted on two crowdsourcing platforms, we investigate an alternative explanation, namely, that the charts allowed participants
       to better assess the drug’s efficacy.

targets.title: Blinded with science: Trivial graphs and formulas increase ad persuasiveness and belief in product efficacy
targets.evidence_quote:
We provide a reappraisal of Tal and Wansink’s study “Blinded with Science”, where seemingly trivial charts were shown
       to increase belief in drug efficacy, presumably because charts are associated with science. Through a series of four replications
       conducted on two crowdsourcing platforms, we investigate an alternative explanation, namely, that the charts allowed participants

targets.outcome_quote:
Meanwhile, we were unable to replicate the original study’s findings, as text with
       chart appeared to be no more persuasive – and sometimes less persuasive – than text alone.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Authors explicitly state that they were unable to replicate the original findings across their experiments; charts did not increase persuasion.

reasoning: Four new-sample experiments retest the two chart experiments from one original paper. Reference-list publication year is 2016 despite the introduction mentioning its 2014 online publication. The formula experiment was excluded.
